concepts.title: Authentication, Authorization, and the Security Filter Chain
concepts.description: Authentication answers the question 'who are you,' authorization answers the separate question 'what are you allowed to do,' and Spring Security enforces both by running every request through a chain of servlet filters that sits in front of your controllers, not inside them.
learningObjectives: Distinguish authentication from authorization with a concrete example of each one failing independently of the other.
Explain, conceptually, what the Spring Security filter chain is and where it sits relative to DispatcherServlet.
Explain the role of the SecurityContext and SecurityContextHolder in carrying the authenticated principal through a request.
Explain which HTTP status results from an authentication failure versus an authorization failure, and why they differ.
Predict how simply adding spring-boot-starter-security to a project changes an application's behavior with zero configuration written.

sections.heading: Two Different Questions: Who Are You, and What Can You Do
sections.body:
**Authentication** answers 'who are you?' -- verifying that a set of presented credentials (a username and password, a bearer token, a client certificate) genuinely corresponds to a real identity. **Authorization** answers a completely separate question: 'given that you are who you say you are, are you allowed to do *this specific thing*?' These two checks are independent, and it's worth internalizing that independence precisely, because conflating them is a common source of confused bug reports: a request can fail authentication (the server has no idea who this is at all) or it can pass authentication but still fail authorization (the server knows exactly who this is, and that identity simply isn't permitted to perform this particular action).

Concretely: a request with no credentials at all, or credentials that don't match any known identity, fails authentication -- the server can't establish who's asking. A request from a perfectly legitimate, successfully-authenticated user -- say, a regular customer -- trying to hit an admin-only endpoint like `DELETE /api/admin/users/7` fails authorization instead: the server knows exactly who's asking, and the answer is 'a real user, but not one permitted to do this.' Getting a login form to work correctly (authentication) and getting role-based access control right (authorization) are genuinely separate engineering problems, even though a single framework -- Spring Security -- handles both.

sections.heading: The Filter Chain: Security Runs Before Your Code Ever Sees the Request
sections.body:
Spring Security is implemented as a chain of servlet `Filter`s, registered at the servlet-container level *in front of* `DispatcherServlet` -- which means security decisions are made before Spring MVC's own routing and handler mapping (covered in the Building REST APIs module) ever runs at all. A rejected request can be turned away before your controller code has any chance to execute, which is precisely the point: security that only kicks in once you're already inside a controller method is security that's trivially easy to accidentally skip on some new endpoint you forget to guard.

Conceptually, a simplified request passes through filters with responsibilities like these, in order: something that extracts and parses credentials from the request (for example, a filter reading a `Authorization: Basic ...` header, or a form-login filter reading posted username/password fields) and attempts to authenticate them; an authorization-decision filter that checks whether the resulting (successful or absent) authentication is permitted to access the specific URL and HTTP method being requested; and an exception-translation filter that catches security-specific failures thrown by any of the above and converts them into the correct HTTP response (`401` or `403`, covered next) rather than letting them propagate as a generic error. Each filter in the chain decides whether to hand the request along to the next one or stop it there -- and only a request that survives every filter in the chain ever reaches `DispatcherServlet` and, eventually, your controller.

sections.heading: SecurityContextHolder and the Authenticated Principal
sections.body:
Once a request is successfully authenticated, Spring Security needs a way to make that fact available to the rest of the request's processing -- your controller, your service layer, method-security checks (covered in the next concept) -- without re-authenticating at every step. It does this with an `Authentication` object: a container holding the identified principal (typically a `UserDetails` implementation, or just a username), the credentials used (usually cleared after authentication succeeds, for safety), and a list of `GrantedAuthority` objects representing what that principal is allowed to do (roles like `ROLE_ADMIN`, or finer-grained permissions).

That `Authentication` object is stored in a `SecurityContext`, which is itself held by `SecurityContextHolder` -- by default backed by a `ThreadLocal`, meaning it's scoped to the single thread handling this one request, populated near the start of the filter chain and available anywhere further downstream in that same thread's call stack, including inside your controller (via an `Authentication` or `Principal` method parameter that Spring MVC resolves for you) or your service layer (via `SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication()` directly). It's cleared at the end of the request specifically so one request's identity can never accidentally leak into another's -- a genuinely important guarantee in a server handling many concurrent requests on a shared thread pool.

sections.heading: What Adding spring-boot-starter-security Changes By Default
sections.body:
Consistent with the autoconfiguration philosophy covered in the Core Concepts module, simply adding `spring-boot-starter-security` as a dependency -- with zero security-specific code written -- changes your application's behavior immediately, because Spring Boot's security autoconfiguration activates the moment the relevant classes appear on the classpath. Specifically: **every endpoint becomes secured by default**, requiring authentication; a default in-memory user named `user` is created automatically, with a randomly generated password that gets printed once, in the startup logs (a line resembling `Using generated security password: 8e557245-...`); and an unauthenticated request to any endpoint is rejected with `401 Unauthorized`, along with (for a browser request) a default login form.

This default, all-or-nothing lockdown is a deliberate, fail-safe design choice -- Spring Boot would rather you notice immediately, loudly, that adding security changed everything, than have you accidentally ship an application with sensitive endpoints wide open because no security configuration happened to exist yet. It is, however, a genuinely common source of confusion the first time a team adds the starter: previously-working, intentionally-public endpoints suddenly all return `401`, with no security configuration class in sight to explain why. The fix -- writing a deliberate `SecurityFilterChain` bean that declares exactly which endpoints should be public and which should require authentication or a specific role -- is the subject of the next concept.

examples.title: Two Requests, Two Different Failure Modes
examples.code:
# Request 1: no credentials supplied at all
GET /api/admin/reports HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com

# Response: 401 Unauthorized
# -- Spring Security has no idea who is making this request at all.


# Request 2: valid credentials for a real, authenticated user -- but that
# user only has ROLE_CUSTOMER, and this endpoint requires ROLE_ADMIN
GET /api/admin/reports HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Authorization: Basic YW15OnBhc3N3b3JkMTIz

# Response: 403 Forbidden
# -- Spring Security knows exactly who this is; that identity is simply
# not permitted to access this specific resource.
examples.explanation: Both requests are rejected, but for genuinely different reasons that map to different HTTP statuses. The first request fails authentication entirely -- there's no Authorization header at all, so the server cannot establish an identity, and 401 Unauthorized is the correct, standard response for 'you have not proven who you are.' The second request succeeds at authentication (the credentials are valid and correspond to a real, known user) but fails authorization -- the authenticated identity's granted authorities don't include whatever this endpoint's access rule requires, and 403 Forbidden is the correct response for 'you are known, but you are not allowed to do this.' Conflating these two failure modes into a single generic error response would hide genuinely useful diagnostic information from both developers and, within reason, legitimate API consumers.

examples.title: The Filter Chain, Conceptually, Ahead of DispatcherServlet
examples.explanation: This is a simplified, conceptual ordering of responsibilities rather than an exhaustive or exact list of Spring Security's internal filter classes, but the structure it illustrates is real and important: authentication-related filters run, then an authorization decision is made, then any security-specific exception from either stage gets translated into the right HTTP status -- and every one of these steps happens before DispatcherServlet, the class responsible for routing to your controllers, is ever invoked. A request that gets turned away at step 2 or step 3 never reaches step 5 at all; your controller method's body simply never runs, which is exactly why relying on an if-check inside a controller method to enforce security would be both redundant with, and strictly weaker than, enforcement at this earlier, unavoidable layer.

examples.title: Reading the Authenticated Principal Inside a Controller
examples.explanation: Spring MVC recognizes Authentication and Principal as special argument types it can resolve automatically for a controller method, without any @RequestParam-style annotation -- it fetches the current Authentication straight out of SecurityContextHolder (specifically, the SecurityContext for this request's thread) and hands it in. By the time this method runs, the filter chain has already established who this request belongs to; the controller doesn't authenticate anything itself, it simply reads the identity the filter chain already determined. This is the concrete, practical payoff of SecurityContextHolder existing: any code running later in the same request's thread -- controller, service, or otherwise -- can ask 'who is this?' without needing to re-run any authentication logic.

misconceptions.description: Authentication and authorization are basically the same concept -- just two different words people use interchangeably for 'security.'
misconceptions.clarification: They answer genuinely different questions and fail in genuinely different, independently-observable ways. Authentication establishes identity: who is making this request, verified via credentials. Authorization is a separate decision made AFTER identity is established: is this specific, now-known identity permitted to perform this specific action or access this specific resource. A request can fail one without failing the other -- a fully authenticated, legitimate user can still be correctly denied access to an admin-only endpoint (authorization failure, 403), while a request with no credentials at all never even gets to the point of an authorization decision, because there's no identity yet to evaluate (authentication failure, 401).

misconceptions.description: Spring Security only actually takes effect once a request reaches your controller method, so an if-check inside the method body is a reliable way to fully secure an endpoint.
misconceptions.clarification: Spring Security is implemented as a chain of servlet filters that runs at the servlet-container level, strictly BEFORE DispatcherServlet -- and therefore before ANY controller method -- ever gets a chance to execute. A request that fails authentication or authorization is turned away by the filter chain itself; the controller method's body never runs at all in that case, so there's nothing for an if-check inside it to even guard against for that particular failure. Relying on manual in-method checks as the primary security mechanism is strictly weaker than configuring the filter chain correctly (the subject of the next concept), because it's trivially easy to forget the check on some new endpoint, whereas a correctly configured, centralized filter-chain rule applies automatically to every request that matches it, with no per-method code required at all.

exercises.prompt:
A REST API has an endpoint GET /api/admin/audit-log that requires the caller to be authenticated AND to hold ROLE_ADMIN. Predict the HTTP status for each of these two requests, and explain why they differ.

Request A: sent with no Authorization header at all.
Request B: sent with a valid Authorization header for a real, successfully-authenticated user who only holds ROLE_CUSTOMER.
exercises.code:
// Request A
GET /api/admin/audit-log HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com

// Request B
GET /api/admin/audit-log HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Authorization: Basic <valid credentials for a ROLE_CUSTOMER user>
hints: For Request A, can the server establish any identity at all from what was sent? If not, which of the two security questions (authn or authz) never even gets a chance to be asked?
For Request B, the server CAN establish a real identity -- so does it fail at the 'who are you' stage, or at the 'what are you allowed to do' stage?
401 corresponds to one of these two questions failing; 403 corresponds to the other. Match each request to the specific question it fails.
exercises.expectedAnswer: Request A returns 401 Unauthorized, because no credentials were supplied at all -- the server cannot establish any identity, so authentication itself fails before an authorization decision is even possible. Request B returns 403 Forbidden, because the credentials ARE valid and correspond to a real, known user (authentication succeeds), but that user's granted authorities (ROLE_CUSTOMER) don't satisfy this endpoint's requirement of ROLE_ADMIN, so the request is correctly denied at the authorization stage instead.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The two requests fail at two different, sequential stages of the filter chain. Request A never even reaches an authorization decision, because there's no credential to authenticate in the first place -- the authentication stage itself fails, and Spring Security's exception-translation filter converts that into 401 Unauthorized, the standard response for 'you have not established who you are.' Request B's credentials ARE valid, so the authentication stage succeeds and a real Authentication object, with ROLE_CUSTOMER among its granted authorities, is placed into the SecurityContext for this request. The authorization stage then runs next, checks that authority list against this endpoint's requirement (ROLE_ADMIN), finds no match, and denies the request -- resulting in 403 Forbidden, the standard response for 'you are known, but not permitted to do this.' The distinction matters in practice because a client encountering 401 knows it needs to (re-)authenticate, while a client encountering 403 knows re-authenticating as the SAME user won't help at all -- a fundamentally different signal to act on.

exercises.prompt: A team adds spring-boot-starter-security to their project's build file to prepare for adding real login functionality later. After restarting the application, every single endpoint -- including ones that were always meant to be public, like GET /api/health -- now returns 401 Unauthorized, and no security configuration class exists anywhere in the codebase yet. Explain what's actually happening, and describe, at a high level, the shape of the fix (full implementation is covered in the next concept).
hints: This isn't a bug in the traditional sense -- nothing is broken. What does Spring Boot's security autoconfiguration do by default the moment the starter is present on the classpath, with zero configuration written?
The generated password log line is a strong clue about what default behavior just activated -- a default in-memory user was created, and every endpoint now requires SOME authenticated identity.

The actual fix isn't about removing the starter -- it's about writing an explicit SecurityFilterChain bean that declares GET /api/health (and any other genuinely public endpoints) as permitAll(), while requiring authentication for the rest. That's the subject of the next concept.
exercises.solutionExplanation: This is Spring Boot's intended, fail-safe default: the moment spring-boot-starter-security is on the classpath, its security autoconfiguration activates and locks down EVERY endpoint behind authentication by default, creates a single in-memory user named 'user' with a randomly generated password (printed once, in the startup logs, specifically so someone can actually log in and confirm security really is active), and rejects any unauthenticated request with 401. This is deliberate: Spring Boot would rather an entire application become suddenly, loudly inaccessible the moment security is added than have a team assume 'we added the dependency, so we must be secure now' while some endpoint stays accidentally, silently open. Nothing is actually broken -- the team simply hasn't yet written the configuration that declares which endpoints, like /api/health, should be genuinely public. The real fix is to define a SecurityFilterChain bean using HttpSecurity that explicitly marks specific paths as permitAll() and leaves (or explicitly marks) the rest as requiring authentication -- replacing the blanket default lockdown with a deliberate, reviewable policy, which is exactly the subject of the next concept.

assessments.prompt: A request to a protected endpoint includes valid, correctly-verified credentials for a real user account, but that user's role does not permit the specific action being requested. What HTTP status should the server return, and why?
options: 401 Unauthorized, because the user is still not permitted to complete the request, which is what 'unauthorized' means.
403 Forbidden, because authentication succeeded (the identity is genuinely known and verified) but authorization failed -- the known identity simply isn't permitted to perform this action.
500 Internal Server Error, because a mismatch between a user's role and the requested action indicates a server-side configuration bug.
200 OK with an error message in the response body, since the request itself was well-formed and reached a real endpoint.
assessments.explanation: Authentication and authorization are distinct checks that can succeed or fail independently. Here, authentication clearly succeeds -- the credentials are valid and correspond to a real, known identity -- so a 401, which specifically signals a failure to establish identity at all, would be misleading despite its name containing 'unauthorized.' The failure here is squarely at the authorization stage: the now-known identity's granted authorities don't satisfy what this specific action requires, which is precisely the scenario 403 Forbidden exists to describe. Option C is wrong -- this is an entirely expected, correctly-functioning access-control outcome, not a bug. Option D is wrong -- silently returning 200 for a denied request would hide a real access-control decision from the client and any tooling inspecting response codes.

assessments.prompt: Explain to a developer who has never worked with Spring Security before what the filter chain is, why it runs where it does relative to DispatcherServlet, and how the SecurityContextHolder lets later code know who's making the current request without re-authenticating.
assessments.modelAnswer: Spring Security is built as a sequence of ordinary servlet filters -- the same general mechanism Java's servlet API has always provided for code that needs to run against every incoming request before it reaches an application's actual handling logic. Crucially, this filter chain is registered at the servlet-container level, positioned in front of DispatcherServlet, the single servlet responsible for routing requests to your @RestController methods. That positioning is deliberate and important: it means every security decision -- verifying who's making the request, and then deciding whether that identity is allowed to do what it's asking to do -- happens BEFORE Spring MVC's own routing and handler-mapping logic ever runs, and therefore before any of your own controller code has a chance to execute at all. A request that the filter chain decides to reject, for either reason, simply never reaches your application's business logic; there is no scenario where an attacker or an unauthorized caller 'slips past' security by hitting some controller method directly, because the controller method is unreachable except by first passing through the entire chain. Within that chain, one stage is responsible for authentication -- extracting whatever credentials the request presents (a header, a cookie, posted form fields, depending on how the app is configured) and verifying them against a known set of identities -- and, on success, packages the result into an Authentication object: an identity, its granted authorities (roles/permissions), and (usually cleared) credentials. That object is stored in a SecurityContext, which SecurityContextHolder makes available for the remainder of that request's processing, on that same thread -- by default via a ThreadLocal, meaning it's scoped precisely to the one request currently being handled and automatically cleared once that request finishes, so there's no risk of one request's identity leaking into another's on a shared thread pool. This is exactly why a controller method, or a service method further down the call stack, can simply ask 'who is the current user?' (via an Authentication or Principal parameter, or by reaching into SecurityContextHolder directly) without needing to perform any authentication logic itself -- that work already happened, once, earlier in the same request's journey through the filter chain, and the result is just sitting there, already resolved, waiting to be read.

concepts.title: Securing Endpoints with HttpSecurity and Method Security
concepts.description: HttpSecurity lets you declare, in one place, exactly which URL patterns are public and which require authentication or a specific role, while method-security annotations like @PreAuthorize push that same access-control decision down onto individual service methods -- two complementary tools for two different levels of granularity.
learningObjectives: Configure a SecurityFilterChain bean using HttpSecurity to permit certain paths and require authentication or a specific role for others.
Explain why rule order matters within authorizeHttpRequests and predict which of two overlapping rules wins for a given request.
Use @PreAuthorize for method-level authorization and explain how it differs in granularity from URL-based HttpSecurity rules.
Explain why @EnableMethodSecurity is required for @PreAuthorize to have any effect, and what happens -- silently -- if it's forgotten.
Explain the self-invocation limitation of proxy-based method security as a known edge case.

sections.heading: Declaring URL-Level Rules with HttpSecurity
From WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter to a SecurityFilterChain Bean
sections.body: Older Spring Security tutorials and codebases configure security by extending a base class, `WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter`, and overriding a `configure(HttpSecurity http)` method. That class was deprecated starting with Spring Security 5.7 and removed entirely in Spring Security 6, in favor of the `@Bean`-returning-`SecurityFilterChain` style shown above. The motivation lines up with a theme you've already seen elsewhere in this curriculum: Spring Boot generally prefers composition over inheritance-based configuration -- exposing configuration as an explicit `@Bean` rather than requiring you to extend and override a specific base class -- because it's more flexible (a class can't extend more than one base class, but an application can register several independent `SecurityFilterChain` beans, each scoped to a different set of paths via `securityMatcher(...)`, for genuinely different security policies covering different parts of the same application) and more consistent with how the rest of Spring Boot expects you to contribute configuration.

sections.heading: Method Security with @PreAuthorize
@EnableMethodSecurity: The Easy-to-Forget Switch

examples.title: A SecurityFilterChain With Correctly Ordered Rules
examples.explanation: Rules are listed from most specific to least specific, which matters because Spring Security evaluates them in order and stops at the first match: /api/public/** is checked first and, for anything under that path, permitAll() wins before the broader rules below it ever get a chance to apply. /api/admin/** requires ROLE_ADMIN specifically. GET requests to /api/orders/** additionally restrict by HTTP method, allowing either CUSTOMER or ADMIN. Finally, anyRequest().authenticated() is the deliberate catch-all, placed last, covering every path not already matched by a more specific rule above it -- requiring at least a valid authenticated identity, with no specific role, for anything left over. @EnableMethodSecurity is also present here, which is what makes @PreAuthorize (used in the next example) actually take effect anywhere in the application.

examples.title: Method Security Enforced Regardless of Caller
examples.explanation: There is no HTTP request or URL involved anywhere in NightlyRefundBatchJob's scheduled call to issueRefund(...) -- so a URL-based HttpSecurity rule restricting /api/refunds/** to ROLE_ADMIN would provide precisely zero protection here, since this call never goes through that URL, or any URL, at all. Because @PreAuthorize is attached directly to issueRefund itself, the same access-control check runs no matter what calls it -- an HTTP-triggered controller, this scheduled job, or any other bean in the application -- which is exactly the scenario where method security earns its place alongside, not instead of, URL-based rules.

examples.title: Rule Order Bug: A Broad Rule Swallowing a Specific One
examples.explanation: In the broken version, anyRequest() -- which, by definition, matches every possible request -- is evaluated first, and because Spring Security stops at the first matching rule, no request ever reaches the /api/public/** rule beneath it at all; every request, public or not, ends up requiring authentication. This is a purely structural bug: the /api/public/** rule isn't wrong, it's simply dead code from the router's point of view, permanently shadowed by the broader rule placed ahead of it. Swapping the order fixes it with no change to either rule's own logic -- placing the specific rule first ensures it gets evaluated, and matched, before the broad catch-all ever has a chance to claim that same request.

misconceptions.description: Rules inside authorizeHttpRequests are evaluated as a complete set, and the most specific matching rule always wins automatically, regardless of the order they happen to be written in.
misconceptions.clarification: Spring Security evaluates authorizeHttpRequests rules strictly in the order they're declared and stops at the FIRST rule that matches the request -- there is no automatic 'most specific wins' resolution happening behind the scenes, the way CSS specificity or some routing frameworks work. A broad rule (like a bare anyRequest()) declared before a narrower, more specific one can make that narrower rule completely unreachable, purely because of ordering, even though the narrower rule is, in isolation, perfectly correctly written. The safe convention is to order rules from most specific to least specific, always finishing with a catch-all anyRequest() rule last.

misconceptions.description: @PreAuthorize works automatically the moment it's placed on a method, as long as Spring Security itself is on the classpath and configured somewhere in the app.
misconceptions.clarification: @PreAuthorize requires @EnableMethodSecurity to be present on some @Configuration class before it has ANY effect at all -- without it, the annotation is inert metadata that Spring never reads or acts on, and the annotated method runs completely unguarded for every caller. Critically, there is no error, warning, or startup failure to signal this gap -- the application runs, the code compiles, and the annotation is visibly right there on the method, which is exactly what makes forgetting @EnableMethodSecurity a dangerous, easy-to-miss mistake rather than an obvious one; a passing test that only checks the happy path (an authorized caller succeeding) would never catch it, which is why it's worth specifically testing that an UNauthorized caller is actually rejected.

exercises.prompt: Requests to GET /api/public/status are unexpectedly returning 401 Unauthorized, even though this SecurityFilterChain clearly includes a permitAll() rule for /api/public/**. Find and fix the ordering bug.
hints: authorizeHttpRequests rules are matched in the order they're declared, and evaluation stops at the FIRST rule that matches -- what does anyRequest() match, by definition?
If a rule matching EVERY request is declared first, can any rule declared after it ever actually get evaluated for any request at all?
Reorder the rules so the specific patterns (/api/public/**, /api/admin/**) come before the catch-all anyRequest() rule, which should always be last.
exercises.solutionExplanation: anyRequest() matches literally every request by definition, and because it was declared FIRST, Spring Security's first-match-wins evaluation stops right there for every single request, including ones under /api/public/** -- the permitAll() and hasRole("ADMIN") rules declared afterward are structurally unreachable, since no request can ever fail to match anyRequest() and 'fall through' to them. This is why GET /api/public/status was incorrectly requiring authentication: it matched anyRequest().authenticated() before it ever got a chance to match the intended permitAll() rule. Moving the specific rules ahead of the catch-all, and keeping anyRequest() last, restores the intended behavior: a request to /api/public/** now matches that specific, permissive rule first, before the broader authenticated() rule is ever considered.

exercises.prompt: A ReportService method is annotated @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')"), but a manual test confirms a non-admin user can still call it successfully and get real data back -- the security check appears to be doing nothing at all. Find and fix the bug, given that the SecurityConfig class below is the only security configuration in the application.
hints: @PreAuthorize needs a specific, separate annotation elsewhere in the application before it has any effect at all -- is that annotation present anywhere in SecurityConfig?
Without that annotation, Spring never wraps ReportService in the AOP proxy responsible for actually evaluating @PreAuthorize expressions before a method runs.
Add the missing annotation directly to the SecurityConfig class (or any other @Configuration class) to activate method security application-wide.
exercises.solutionExplanation: @PreAuthorize is inert without @EnableMethodSecurity present on some @Configuration class -- Spring only wraps beans in the AOP proxy responsible for evaluating method-security annotations when explicitly told to via @EnableMethodSecurity, and SecurityConfig here never declared it. Because the proxy was never created, getAllReports() ran exactly like any ordinary, unguarded method for every caller, regardless of role, which is exactly why a non-admin user's manual test call succeeded. Adding @EnableMethodSecurity to SecurityConfig instructs Spring to create that proxy around ReportService (and every other bean with method-security annotations), so calls to getAllReports() are now actually intercepted and evaluated against the current Authentication's granted authorities before the real method body ever executes -- correctly rejecting a caller without ROLE_ADMIN going forward.

assessments.prompt: A SecurityFilterChain declares, in this exact order: (1) requestMatchers("/api/orders/**").hasRole("CUSTOMER"), (2) requestMatchers("/api/orders/summary").permitAll(), (3) anyRequest().authenticated(). A request arrives for GET /api/orders/summary. Which rule actually governs this request?
options: Rule 2, because permitAll() always takes precedence over role-based rules regardless of where it's declared.
Rule 1, because it's declared first and its pattern (/api/orders/**) matches /api/orders/summary, and Spring Security stops at the first matching rule.
Rule 3, because anyRequest() is a more general, catch-all rule that Spring Security always evaluates last regardless of declaration order.
All three rules are combined, and the request is permitted only if it satisfies every one of them simultaneously.
assessments.explanation: Spring Security evaluates authorizeHttpRequests rules strictly in declared order and stops at the first match -- there's no rule about permitAll() winning regardless of position (option A is wrong), and anyRequest() isn't automatically deferred to the end unless it's actually written last (option C is wrong here specifically because rule 1 matches first regardless of what's written after it). Since /api/orders/** matches /api/orders/summary and rule 1 is declared before rule 2, rule 1 (hasRole("CUSTOMER")) governs this request, and rule 2's permitAll(), despite looking like it specifically targets this exact path, is unreachable for this request because rule 1 already claimed the match. Option D describes AND-combination semantics Spring Security's rule evaluation does not implement -- exactly one rule applies per request, whichever matches first.

assessments.prompt: Explain the difference between securing an operation with a URL-based rule in HttpSecurity versus securing it with @PreAuthorize on the underlying service method, including a concrete scenario where only one of the two would actually provide protection, and explain the @EnableMethodSecurity requirement.
assessments.modelAnswer: A URL-based rule declared via authorizeHttpRequests on a SecurityFilterChain governs access at the entry point into the application -- it inspects the incoming HTTP request's path and method and decides, before DispatcherServlet even routes the request, whether this specific URL is reachable at all for the current (or absent) authentication. That makes it an excellent, centralized way to lock down an entire area of the API -- 'nothing under /api/admin/** is reachable without ROLE_ADMIN' -- with one rule covering every controller method mapped under that path, regardless of how many there are. But its protection is strictly tied to requests arriving through that URL; it has no visibility into, and provides no protection for, the same underlying business logic being invoked through some other path entirely -- a scheduled job, an internal call from another service bean, a message listener consuming from a queue -- none of which involve an HTTP request or a URL at all. @PreAuthorize, applied directly to the method that implements the sensitive operation, closes exactly that gap: because the check is attached to the operation itself rather than to any particular route into it, it's evaluated identically no matter what actually calls that method, HTTP-triggered or not. In a system with a RefundService.issueRefund(...) method reachable both through a REST endpoint AND through a nightly scheduled batch job, a URL-based rule on the REST endpoint alone would leave the scheduled job's call completely unguarded -- only a @PreAuthorize annotation directly on issueRefund itself protects both call paths uniformly. This protection, however, doesn't activate on its own: @PreAuthorize is just an annotation until @EnableMethodSecurity is declared on some @Configuration class, which is the specific instruction that tells Spring to wrap eligible beans in an AOP proxy capable of intercepting calls and evaluating the annotation's expression before letting the real method run. Forgetting @EnableMethodSecurity produces no error or warning of any kind -- the annotated method simply executes unguarded for every caller -- which makes it a genuinely dangerous, silent gap rather than one that fails loudly and gets noticed immediately.

concepts.title: Password Hashing with BCrypt
concepts.description: Storing a password requires a slow, automatically-salted, one-way hash like BCrypt rather than plain text or reversible encryption, because an application should never be capable of recovering a user's raw password again -- only of verifying a claimed one.
learningObjectives: Explain why storing passwords in plain text, or with reversible encryption, is wrong even when the database itself is otherwise well protected.
Explain what a one-way hash function is and why irreversibility is the property that actually matters for password storage.
Explain what a salt is, why it defeats precomputed lookup-table attacks, and how BCrypt manages salting automatically.
Explain why BCrypt is deliberately slow via a tunable work factor, and why that slowness is a security feature rather than a performance defect.
Use PasswordEncoder.encode() and matches() correctly, and explain why comparing two independently-produced hashes with plain string equality is not a reliable way to verify a password.

sections.heading: Why Plain Text and Reversible Encryption Are Both Wrong
sections.body:
Storing a user's password as plain text means that anyone who can read the database -- through a direct breach, an exposed backup, an overly broad internal database permission, or even an accidentally verbose log statement -- reads every single user's real, usable password immediately. Because people reuse passwords across many unrelated services, a leak from one poorly-secured application routinely compromises accounts on entirely unrelated systems too; the damage is never really contained to 'just this one app.'

Reversible *encryption* (as opposed to hashing) looks like an improvement -- the stored value isn't the raw password -- but it only shifts the problem rather than solving it: encryption is designed to be decrypted by whoever holds the right key, and that key has to live *somewhere* the application can reach it, typically in the same configuration or secrets store an attacker who's already breached the application is likely to also gain access to. The deeper principle worth internalizing is this: **a well-designed authentication system should be structurally incapable of recovering a user's original password at all**, ever, under any circumstances -- not 'capable but promising not to,' but genuinely, mathematically unable to. The application's job is only ever to *verify a claim* ('this login attempt supplies the same password that was originally set'), never to *know* the actual password.

sections.heading: One-Way Hashing: Verification Without Reversibility
sections.body:
A cryptographic hash function takes an input of any size and deterministically produces a fixed-size output (the *hash* or *digest*) with a critical property: it is computationally infeasible to work backward from the output to recover the original input. 'Deterministic' matters here too -- the same input always produces the exact same output, which is precisely what makes verification possible at all: to check a login attempt, the application hashes the *newly entered* password and compares that fresh hash against the *previously stored* hash from registration -- it never attempts to decrypt or recover the original stored value, because with a proper one-way hash, there is no operation that could do that even in principle.

This reframes the entire authentication problem: registration stores `hash(password)`, never `password` itself; login re-derives `hash(entered_password)` and compares it against the stored value. If the two hashes match, the entered password was (almost certainly) the same string that produced that stored hash in the first place -- verification achieved with zero moments in the process where the raw password needed to be retained anywhere beyond the instant it was typed.

sections.heading: Salting: Defeating Precomputed Lookup Tables
sections.body:
A plain, unsalted hash has a specific, exploitable weakness: identical passwords always produce identical hashes. This means an attacker who obtains a breached database of hashes doesn't need to attack each one individually -- they can precompute hashes for millions of common passwords once (a *rainbow table*) and then simply look up any hash from the breach against that table, instantly recovering every user whose password happened to be common, all at once, for the cost of building the table a single time.

A **salt** is random data mixed into the password before hashing, specifically to defeat this: `hash(password + salt)` produces a different result for the same password whenever the salt differs, so a precomputed table built for one salt is useless against a hash produced with a different one. BCrypt handles this automatically and safely: every time you call `encode(rawPassword)`, it generates a fresh, random salt internally and bakes it directly into its own output string -- you never manage a separate salt column or generate one yourself. A BCrypt hash string looks like `$2a$10$N9qo8uLOickgx2ZMRZoMyeIjZAgcfl7p92ldGxad68LJZdL17lhWy`, where `$2a$` identifies the algorithm version, `10` is the cost/work factor (covered next), and the remainder of the string encodes both the salt and the actual hash together, concatenated -- which is exactly why `matches(rawPassword, storedHash)` can extract the original salt straight back out of the stored hash itself before re-hashing the candidate password with that same salt for comparison.

sections.heading: Deliberately Slow: The Work Factor as a Feature, Not a Bug
sections.body:
General-purpose hash functions like MD5 or plain SHA-256 are explicitly *fast* -- that's exactly what makes them excellent for their intended purposes (checksums, data structure lookups) and exactly what makes them dangerous for password storage. An attacker who obtains a breached database of fast-hashed passwords can attempt billions of guesses per second on modern GPU hardware, making brute-force and dictionary attacks against the entire leaked database genuinely practical, even against hashes that were properly salted.

BCrypt is deliberately, intentionally slow, via a configurable **work factor** (also called the cost or strength parameter -- the `10` in the example hash string above) that controls how many internal rounds of computation each single hash operation performs. Doubling the work factor roughly doubles the time each hash takes. For one real login attempt, this added cost is negligible -- a few extra milliseconds a genuine user will never notice. But for an attacker attempting billions of guesses against a leaked hash database, that same per-hash cost, multiplied across billions of attempts, becomes the difference between a brute-force attack finishing in hours versus centuries. Spring Security's `BCryptPasswordEncoder` defaults to a reasonable work factor (10, as of recent versions) but the constructor accepts an explicit strength argument, and the accepted industry guidance is to periodically *increase* it over time as hardware gets faster -- never to lower it in the name of shaving milliseconds off a login endpoint's response time, which would be trading away the entire point of using BCrypt in the first place.

examples.title: Encoding a Password at Registration
examples.explanation: PasswordEncoder is exposed as an ordinary @Bean, exactly like any other bean covered in the Core Concepts module, so it can be constructor-injected into any service that needs it -- there's nothing special about how it's wired in. encode(rawPassword) generates a fresh random salt internally and produces a BCrypt hash string with that salt embedded in it; that hash string -- and only that hash string -- is what gets persisted. The raw password exists only transiently, for the duration of this method call, and is never written to the database, a log, or anywhere else that would outlive this request.

examples.title: Verifying a Login Attempt Correctly, and the Wrong Way to Try
examples.explanation: matches(rawPassword, storedHash) is specifically designed for this comparison: it reads the salt and work factor that are already embedded in storedHash, re-hashes rawPassword using that exact same salt and work factor, and only then compares the two resulting hash values -- correctly returning true whenever the candidate password matches, regardless of what a fresh, independently-generated hash of the same password would look like. The commented-out WRONG approach calls encode(rawPassword) a second, entirely separate time, which generates a brand new random salt unrelated to the one already stored -- producing a hash that will differ from the stored one essentially every time, even for the exact correct password, because BCrypt hashes of the same input differ whenever their salts differ.

examples.title: Two Hashes of the Same Password, Deliberately Different
examples.explanation: hash1 and hash2 are produced by encoding the exact same string, "password123", twice -- and yet they look nothing alike, because each call to encode() generates its own fresh, random salt, and that salt is baked directly into the resulting string. hash1.equals(hash2) is false, which is completely expected and NOT a bug -- it's the direct, intended consequence of per-call random salting. Both matches(...) calls nonetheless correctly return true, because each one independently extracts the specific salt embedded in its own stored hash argument and re-hashes "password123" with that particular salt before comparing -- proving that verification never depends on two independently-produced hashes looking identical to each other at all.

misconceptions.description: You can verify a login attempt by hashing the entered password yourself with encode(...) and comparing it to the stored hash using .equals() or ==.
misconceptions.clarification: Every call to a BCryptPasswordEncoder's encode() method generates a brand-new, random salt, so hashing the same password twice produces two visibly different strings almost every time -- comparing a freshly-encoded hash to a previously-stored one with .equals() will fail even when the password is genuinely, exactly correct. The correct approach is passwordEncoder.matches(rawPassword, storedHash), which specifically extracts the salt already embedded in the STORED hash and re-hashes the candidate password using that same salt before comparing -- this is precisely why matches() takes both the raw candidate and the stored hash as separate arguments, rather than just comparing two hashes directly.

misconceptions.description: BCrypt being slow is a performance problem worth working around, for example by lowering its work factor (cost/strength) to make login endpoints respond faster.
misconceptions.clarification: BCrypt's slowness is a deliberate, load-bearing security property, not an implementation inefficiency to be optimized away. The added computation cost per hash is negligible for a single genuine login attempt (a few extra milliseconds, unnoticeable to a real user) but becomes the dominant, crippling cost for an attacker attempting billions of guesses against a breached database of hashes -- lowering the work factor to shave milliseconds off a login endpoint directly and proportionally weakens that protection against offline brute-force attacks. The accepted, recommended practice is the opposite: periodically INCREASING the work factor over time as hardware gets faster, to keep the same effective level of protection rather than let it silently erode.

exercises.prompt: This login method rejects every login attempt as invalid, even when the user enters their password correctly. Find and fix the bug.
hints: encode(...) is called here on every single login attempt -- does BCrypt's encode() produce the exact same output string for the same input every time it's called, or does something change between calls?
Compare this to how the password was originally stored at registration time -- was that stored value produced by this same encode() call, using the same salt?
There's a purpose-built method on PasswordEncoder specifically designed to compare a raw candidate password against an already-stored hash, without needing to generate a matching salt yourself.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original code calls passwordEncoder.encode(rawPassword) fresh, on every login attempt, which generates a brand-new random salt each time -- completely unrelated to whatever salt was embedded in the hash stored at registration. Comparing that freshly-generated hash against the stored one with .equals() will essentially always return false, since two BCrypt hashes of the same password produced with two different random salts look nothing alike, regardless of whether the entered password is correct. The fix replaces this with passwordEncoder.matches(rawPassword, user.getHashedPassword()), which correctly extracts the salt already embedded in the STORED hash, re-hashes the candidate rawPassword using that exact same salt, and only then compares -- which is the only mechanism that can correctly verify a password without ever needing the original raw password to have been retained anywhere.

exercises.prompt: A user's password "correcthorse" was hashed at registration and stored as storedHash. Later, an attacker who has stolen the database tries to brute-force it by calling passwordEncoder.encode("correcthorse") themselves and comparing the result to storedHash using .equals(). Separately, the real login flow calls passwordEncoder.matches("correcthorse", storedHash). Predict the result of each comparison, and explain why they differ despite both starting from the exact correct password.
hints: The attacker's encode("correcthorse") call generates its own brand-new random salt -- is there any reason to expect it would coincidentally match the salt embedded in storedHash from registration?
matches(...) doesn't generate a new salt at all -- it reads whichever salt is already embedded in the storedHash argument you give it.
Both comparisons start from the objectively correct password -- the difference in outcome comes entirely from HOW each one performs its comparison, not from the password being right or wrong.
exercises.expectedAnswer: attackerCheck is (almost certainly) false, because encode("correcthorse") called a second time generates a brand-new, unrelated random salt, producing a hash string that looks nothing like storedHash even though the underlying password is identical. loginCheck is true, because matches(...) extracts the salt already embedded in storedHash itself and re-hashes "correcthorse" using that exact same salt before comparing, which correctly confirms the password matches regardless of what a fresh, independently-salted encode() call would produce.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The attacker's approach fundamentally misunderstands what BCrypt guarantees: encode("correcthorse") does not produce a stable, repeatable 'fingerprint' of the string "correcthorse" -- it produces a hash tied to whatever fresh, random salt happens to be generated on that particular call, and two separate calls to encode() with the identical input produce two different salts and therefore two different-looking hash strings almost every single time. Comparing the attacker's freshly-generated hash to storedHash with .equals() is comparing two hashes built from two unrelated salts, so it fails regardless of whether the underlying password is correct -- this is precisely why a stolen hash database can't be attacked by simply re-hashing guesses and directly comparing the resulting strings. The real login flow avoids this entirely by using matches(rawPassword, storedHash), which reads the salt that's already embedded directly inside storedHash (this is exactly what BCrypt's own hash format is designed to make possible) and re-hashes the candidate password using that identical salt before comparing -- the only correct way to verify a BCrypt-hashed password, and the reason PasswordEncoder exposes matches() as a distinct method rather than expecting callers to compare two encode() outputs directly.

assessments.prompt: Calling passwordEncoder.encode("hunter2") twice, back to back, produces two completely different-looking output strings. What is the most accurate explanation, and is this a bug?
options: It's a bug -- a correctly implemented password encoder should produce the identical hash for the identical input every time.

It's expected, intended behavior -- each call generates a fresh, random salt that gets embedded in the output, so identical inputs produce different-looking hashes on purpose, specifically to defeat precomputed lookup-table attacks.
It's expected, but only because "hunter2" is a well-known example password that BCrypt specifically randomizes further as an extra precaution.
It indicates the PasswordEncoder bean was misconfigured with an inconsistent work factor between the two calls.
assessments.explanation: BCrypt is specifically designed so that encode() generates a new random salt on every call and bakes that salt directly into the returned hash string -- this is intentional, not a bug, and it's exactly what defeats precomputed rainbow-table attacks: an attacker can't precompute one hash per common password and expect it to match, because the salt varies every time a hash is produced. Option A is wrong because that 'correctly implemented' behavior it describes is precisely the UNSAFE, unsalted behavior real password hashing deliberately avoids. Option C is wrong -- there's nothing special-cased about any particular password string; every input is salted identically. Option D is wrong -- nothing about this behavior implies misconfiguration; it would happen with any correctly configured BCryptPasswordEncoder, at any consistent work factor.

assessments.prompt: A junior developer suggests storing passwords with a reversible encryption scheme instead of BCrypt, reasoning that 'if we ever need to recover a user's password for support purposes, we can just decrypt it.' Explain why this reasoning is flawed, and explain how BCrypt's salting and deliberate slowness address the real underlying risks that plain or reversible storage doesn't.
assessments.modelAnswer: The junior developer's reasoning treats 'being able to recover the original password' as a feature, but for password storage specifically, that capability is itself the core risk, not a convenience worth preserving. A well-designed authentication system should never need to know a user's actual password after the moment it was first set -- its only job afterward is to verify a CLAIM ('this new login attempt supplies the same password as before'), and that verification can be done perfectly well without ever being able to reconstruct the original string. Reversible encryption keeps that reconstruction possible by definition -- decryption exists precisely to reverse it -- which means the decryption key has to be available to the application somewhere, and anyone who compromises the application (the same attacker who presumably already breached the database to get at the encrypted passwords in the first place) is very likely to also be able to reach that key, at which point every single stored password is recoverable in one step. This doesn't actually solve the problem plain-text storage has; it just adds one extra step an attacker with real access has to perform. A one-way hash function like BCrypt sidesteps this entirely by being, by design, computationally infeasible to reverse -- there is no key anywhere that could 'decrypt' a BCrypt hash back into the original password, because the operation genuinely only goes one direction. Verification instead re-hashes a fresh login attempt and compares it against the stored hash, which needs no reversal at all. On top of that one-way property, BCrypt adds two further protections that plain hashing alone wouldn't provide: it automatically generates and embeds a random salt into every hash it produces, ensuring that even two users who happen to choose the identical password end up with completely different stored hashes -- which defeats an attacker's ability to precompute a lookup table of hashes for common passwords and instantly recognize matches across an entire breached database. And it deliberately makes each individual hash computation slow, via a tunable work factor, which costs a genuine user an imperceptible few milliseconds per login but multiplies into a crippling amount of total compute time for an attacker attempting billions of guesses against a stolen hash database. Together, one-way irreversibility, per-password random salting, and deliberate computational slowness directly address the three realistic threats a breached password store actually faces -- recovery, precomputed lookup, and brute force -- in a way that plain text or reversible encryption simply cannot, no matter how well-intentioned the 'just in case we need to recover it' reasoning sounds.
